claims.text: The initial non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous metastable solid solution.
Thermal aging induces phase separation in the alloy.
Mg preferentially segregates to grain boundaries during thermal aging.
Mg segregation produces localized Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
Mg-rich precipitates act as nucleation sites for a continuous protective MgO or Mg-containing spinel layer.
The precipitate-assisted oxide layer reduces the high-temperature oxidation rate.
The precipitate-assisted oxide layer enhances corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Rapid solidification or similar non-equilibrium processing yields a mixed solid-solution/intermetallic precursor without developed grain-boundary segregation.
Sub-transus thermal aging can stimulate phase separation and precipitate formation without fully equilibrating the alloy.
Enhanced Mg diffusion causes Mg segregation and nucleation of Mg-rich precipitates.
Mg-rich precipitates oxidize preferentially because of their high Mg content.
Preferential oxidation of Mg-rich precipitates generates a coherent and adherent MgO or Mg-containing spinel scale.
The coherent oxide scale acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and corrosive attack.
The aged alloy will have a lower TGA-measured high-temperature oxidation rate than the as-cast baseline.
The aged alloy will have better electrochemically measured corrosion resistance than the as-cast baseline.
The as-cast baseline has a relatively uniform Mg distribution without significant localized or grain-boundary segregation.
The as-cast baseline forms a less protective, discontinuous oxide layer during high-temperature exposure.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes the initial alloy as a homogeneous metastable solid solution, whereas the material_initial_state describes it as a mixed solid-solution/intermetallic precursor.
